title: Light Travels in Straight Lines
keyIdea: Light travels in straight lines from a light source. We see a light source when its light enters our eyes, and we see other objects when light reflects off them into our eyes; eyes do not send light out. Because light cannot bend round an object, an opaque object blocks the rays that hit it and leaves a shadow with the same outline as the object. Moving the object closer to the light makes its shadow bigger.
familyTip: In a dark room, shine a torch through holes in three pieces of card lined up in a row, then nudge the middle one sideways and watch the light vanish. Then make hand shadows on a wall and move your hand towards and away from the torch. Ask each time: where do the straight rays go?

visual.caption: True or false? Drag each statement to a box, or tap it and then tap a box.

items: Our eyes send out light so we can see
We see a book because light bounces off it into our eyes
A shadow has the same outline as the object
Light bends round objects to fill in shadows
Moving a toy closer to the torch makes its shadow bigger

lab.caption: Flagship lab: line up holed cards, build the ray path for seeing a book, make shaped shadows, resize a shadow, and predict where its edge falls.

kid: Light travels in straight lines. It cannot bend round corners. That is why you cannot see round a corner.
We see a lamp because its light travels straight into our eyes. We see a book because light from the lamp bounces off the book and then travels into our eyes. Our eyes do not send out light.
When something blocks the light, it makes a shadow. The rays that just miss the edge go straight on. So the shadow has the same outline as the thing that made it.
Move a toy closer to the torch and it blocks more of the spreading rays. Its shadow gets bigger. Move it closer to the wall and the shadow gets smaller.
adult: Ages 10 to 11. This is the Year 6 Light unit in the National Curriculum in England. Pupils recognise that light appears to travel in straight lines. They use this idea to explain that objects are seen because they give out or reflect light into the eye. They also use it to explain why shadows have the same shape as the objects that cast them. Key words: light source, ray, ray diagram, reflect, opaque, shadow, straight line.

Ray diagrams model light as straight lines with arrows pointing away from the source. To see a lit object, draw a ray from the source to the object and a second ray from the object to the eye. A small source gives a sharp shadow. Its size follows similar triangles: shadow height equals object height times the source-to-screen distance divided by the source-to-object distance.

Common mistakes: drawing the arrows from the eye to the object, as if eyes send out light; thinking we see objects without any light reaching the eye; thinking light bends round objects or fills in shadows; and thinking a shadow is a kind of reflection. Many children also expect a shadow to shrink as the object nears the light, when it grows.

In the lab your child lines up three holed cards so the beam reaches an eye, builds the ray paths for seeing a lamp and a book, swaps shaped cards to see matching shadows, slides a card to make its shadow twice as tall and then nearly card-sized, and predicts where a shadow's top edge will fall before switching on.

practice.prompt: Three cards with holes are lined up between a torch and your eye. The middle card moves sideways. What happens?
choices: The light bends to find the hole
practice.hint: Can light change direction to go through a hole that is off the line?
practice.explain: Light travels in straight lines, so it cannot reach a hole that is off the line. The card blocks it.

practice.prompt: In a ray diagram for seeing a book, which way should the arrows point?
choices: Lamp to book, then book to eye
practice.hint: Where does the light start? Where does it end?
practice.explain: Light starts at the source, bounces off the book and ends in the eye. Arrows show that direction.

practice.prompt: A card {h} cm tall is halfway between a small torch and a wall. How tall is its shadow on the wall, in cm?
practice.hint: The rays spread out in straight lines. By the wall they have gone twice as far as at the card.
practice.explain: The wall is twice as far from the torch as the card is, so the shadow is twice as tall: 2 × {h} = {=2*h} cm.

practice.prompt: Why does a cat-shaped card make a cat-shaped shadow?
choices: Rays that just miss its edges go straight on
The card reflects a picture of itself
practice.hint: What happens to the rays that do not hit the card?
practice.explain: Rays that hit the card are blocked; rays that just miss its edges travel straight on. That traces the card's outline.

practice.prompt: A card {h} cm tall is a third of the way from a small torch to a wall. How tall is its shadow, in cm?
practice.hint: By the wall, the rays have travelled three times as far as at the card, so they have spread three times as much.
practice.explain: The wall is 3 times as far from the torch as the card, so the shadow is 3 × {h} = {=3*h} cm tall.

pool.prompt: Why can you not see round a corner?
pool.hint: Think about the shape of the path light takes.
pool.explain: Light travels in straight lines, so light from round the corner cannot turn to reach your eyes.

pool.prompt: How do you see a book in a lit room?
choices: Light bounces off it into your eyes
Light leaves your eyes and hits it
The book gives out its own light
pool.hint: Is a book a light source?
pool.explain: The book is not a light source. Light from a lamp or the Sun reflects off it and travels into your eyes.

pool.prompt: You move your hand closer to a torch. What happens to its shadow on the wall?
pool.hint: Near the torch, does your hand block a wide spread of rays or a narrow one?
pool.explain: Close to the torch, the hand blocks a wide fan of rays, so the shadow gets bigger.

pool.prompt: Ella says a shadow is a reflection of the object. Is she right?
choices: No, it is where light is blocked
Yes, the object reflects its shape
pool.hint: Is there more light or less light in a shadow?
pool.explain: A shadow is a dark area where an opaque object blocks the light. It is not a reflection.

pool.prompt: In a dark room with no light at all, can you see a red book?
choices: No, no light reaches your eyes from it
pool.hint: What has to enter your eyes for you to see something?
pool.explain: You see things only when light from them enters your eyes. With no light, the book cannot reflect any.

pool.prompt: A toy {h} cm tall is a quarter of the way from a small lamp to a wall. How tall is its shadow, in cm?
pool.hint: By the wall, the rays have gone 4 times as far as at the toy.
pool.explain: The wall is 4 times as far from the lamp as the toy, so the shadow is 4 × {h} = {=4*h} cm.

pool.prompt: Which object makes its own light?
pool.hint: A light source gives out light; other things only reflect it.
pool.explain: A torch is a light source. A mirror and the Moon only reflect light that comes from somewhere else.

pool.prompt: A card is {h} cm tall. Its shadow is {=2*h} cm tall. How many times as far from the torch is the wall as the card?
pool.hint: Compare the shadow height with the card height.
pool.explain: {=2*h} ÷ {h} = 2, so the wall is twice as far from the torch as the card. Shadow size grows with distance in straight lines.

pool.prompt: A laser beam in a smoky room looks like a straight line. What does this show?
pool.hint: The smoke lets you see the path of the light.
pool.explain: Smoke scatters a little light to your eyes from all along the beam, showing its path is straight.
